title: Star Formation
body:
A star forms when a cold cloud in the interstellar medium collapses under its own gravity. The
medium is thin gas and dust between the stars, mostly hydrogen, at temperatures low enough that
gravity can overcome the pressure resisting collapse.

The collapse has three consequences worth naming:

```
angular momentum is conserved   the cloud spins faster as it shrinks, and flattens
                                into a disc, which is why planetary systems are flat

gravitational energy becomes    compression heats the core long before fusion starts
heat

fragmentation                   a large cloud collapses into many cores, so stars
                                form in clusters
```

The protostar contracts until its core reaches roughly 10 million K, at which point hydrogen
fusion begins and the outward pressure it generates halts the collapse. That balance is
hydrostatic equilibrium, gravity inward against pressure outward, and it is a
[[Free-Body Diagram]] written for a shell of gas. The star has then joined the
[[Main Sequence]].

Below about 0.08 solar masses the core never gets hot enough and the object becomes a brown
dwarf, which is the lower boundary of what counts as a star.
